title: NEET UG 2026 - Medical Entrance for MBBS, BDS & AYUSH
meta_description: NEET UG 2026 - medical entrance exam for MBBS, BDS, AYUSH. NTA exam pattern, syllabus, cutoff, counselling process, and preparation.

hero.one_liner: India's single medical entrance exam - NEET UG is the only gateway to MBBS, BDS, and AYUSH admissions in all government and private medical colleges.

what_is_it: NEET UG (National Eligibility cum Entrance Test - Undergraduate) is India's single entrance exam for admission to MBBS, BDS, BAMS (Ayurveda), BHMS (Homeopathy), BUMS (Unani), and related medical/dental/AYUSH courses in all government and private medical colleges across India (excluding only AIIMS and JIPMER, which now accept NEET scores too). With 24+ lakh applicants competing for approximately 1,10,000 MBBS seats, NEET is India's largest entrance exam by sheer number of candidates - more than JEE Main. It is conducted once per year in pen-and-paper mode (OMR sheet), not online.

NEET score is the determining factor for admission to: Government medical colleges through state quota and All-India Quota (AIQ), Private medical colleges, Deemed universities with medical programs, AIIMS institutions (post-acceptance of NEET), JIPMER (post-acceptance of NEET), and medical colleges abroad recognized by Indian Medical Council. Without NEET qualification, no medical admission is possible in India - NEET is completely monopolistic. The exam tests Physics, Chemistry, and Biology (Botany + Zoology) with 200 MCQs in 3 hours 20 minutes, totaling 720 marks.

NEET 2026 exam is scheduled for May 3, 2026, from 2 to 5 PM. Application registration began February 8, 2026, with the last submission date being March 11, 2026. The exam is conducted in pen-and-paper format using OMR sheets - candidates mark answers in bubble sheets with pencils, unlike modern online exams. This is intentional - OMR format ensures no technical glitches and is equitable for candidates from diverse educational backgrounds. The result is declared typically 2-3 weeks post-exam, followed by state and AIQ counselling in July-August.

Biology dominates NEET scoring - 360 out of 720 marks. Most successful NEET candidates score 320-360 in Biology alone. Physics is the toughest for most aspirants, followed by Chemistry. The qualitative difference: Biology requires depth of knowledge and memory (NCERT-based), Physics requires conceptual clarity (application-based), Chemistry requires balanced memory + concepts. Many students over-prepare Physics while under-preparing Biology - a strategic error. The winner in NEET is who masters Biology first.

key_details.label: Education Requirement
key_details.value: 12th pass with Physics, Chemistry, Biology/Biotechnology. Min 50% aggregate (40% for SC/ST/OBC).

key_details.label: Age Limit
key_details.value: Minimum 17 years as of December 31, 2026. No upper age limit (Supreme Court 2023 ruling).

key_details.label: Exam Attempts
key_details.value: No official limit on number of attempts (as per current rules)

key_details.label: Exam Mode
key_details.value: Offline - Pen and Paper (OMR sheet) - NOT computer-based

exam_pattern.description: 200 MCQs across Physics, Chemistry, Botany, and Zoology. Each subject has Section A (35 questions, compulsory) + Section B (15 questions, attempt any 10). Total questions: 180 (35×4 = 140 compulsory + 40 optional). OMR-based offline exam.
exam_pattern.negative_marking: +4 for each correct answer. -1 for each wrong answer. No marking for unattempted questions.

extra_sections.heading: How NEET leads to a medical seat

steps.title: One exam, 720 marks
steps.desc: A single 3-hour paper of 180 questions decides everything. There is no separate mains or interview.

steps.title: Score, percentile & rank
steps.desc: Your marks convert to a percentile and an all-India rank. Clearing the qualifying percentile makes you eligible for counselling.

steps.title: Counselling (AIQ + State)
steps.desc: You fill choices in All-India Quota and State Quota counselling, across several rounds, based on your rank.

steps.title: MBBS / BDS / AYUSH seat
steps.desc: A seat is allotted by rank, category and your choices. That is where the real medical journey begins.

extra_sections.heading: NEET UG exam pattern - every detail
content: NEET UG has 200 MCQs across Physics (50 questions - attempt 45), Chemistry (50 questions - attempt 45), and Biology (100 questions - attempt 90). Each section is divided into Section A (35 mandatory questions) and Section B (15 questions, attempt 10).
Total marks: 720. Duration: 3 hours 20 minutes.
Marking: +4 correct, -1 wrong. Biology dominates NEET: 90 questions worth 360 marks - exactly 50% of the paper.
Botany and Zoology get 45 questions each. If you score 300+ in Biology alone, you're virtually guaranteed a government medical seat.
Biology is also the most NCERT-dependent - questions are often direct statements from NCERT textbook. Students who memorize NCERT Biology word-by-word score 320-340 in Biology.
Physics is the most challenging section for biology students. Topics like Mechanics, Electrostatics, Optics, and Modern Physics require mathematical problem-solving skills.
However, NEET Physics is significantly easier than JEE Physics - questions test concept application rather than complex multi-step calculations. Chemistry is the easiest section for high scores.

Organic Chemistry (named reactions, reagents, IUPAC naming) and Inorganic Chemistry (periodic trends, p-block, d-block) are heavily NCERT-based. Physical Chemistry requires formula application and calculations but at a straightforward level.

items.title: Biology (360, your score-maker)
items.sub: Read NCERT Class 11 and 12 line by line, several times. Many questions are direct NCERT statements with one word changed.

items.title: Physics (180)
items.sub: Focus on formulae and their application. Mechanics, Electrostatics and Current Electricity, and Modern Physics carry the most marks.

items.title: Chemistry (180)
items.sub: Inorganic is the easiest 60-70 marks, almost pure NCERT. Master named reactions for Organic and 30-40 key formulae for Physical.

items.title: The NCERT habit
items.sub: Five focused readings of NCERT Biology leave you remembering most of the book. One-page notes per chapter make revision fast.

extra_sections.heading: NEET score vs medical college admission
content: Government medical college admission requires: AIQ (All India Quota) - 15% of government seats filled through NEET AIQ counselling by MCC (Medical Counselling Committee). Remaining 85% filled through state-level counselling based on NEET score + domicile.
Getting a government MBBS seat through AIQ typically needs 600+ marks (out of 720) for general category.
State quota cutoffs vary dramatically. In states like UP, Bihar, and Rajasthan (limited government seats, huge applicant pool), you need 580-620 marks for government MBBS.

In states like Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu (more medical colleges), 520-560 may suffice. If you have domicile in a state with lower cutoffs, apply through state counselling for better chances.
Private medical colleges (deemed universities): Admit through NEET score but have higher fees - Rs 10-25 lakh/year for MBBS. Cutoffs are lower (400-500 marks for many private colleges).
If your NEET score is 450-550, a private medical college may be your realistic option. Compare college reputation, clinical exposure, and USMLE/NEXT preparation support before choosing.
AIIMS and JIPMER (now through NEET): Previously separate exams, now merged with NEET. AIIMS Delhi admission requires approximately 700+ marks (top 50 AIR).
Other AIIMS institutions (Jodhpur, Bhopal, Patna) need 680+. These are the most competitive medical seats in India with the best clinical training and research opportunities.

items.title: All-India Quota (15%)
items.sub: 15% of government college seats, allotted by all-India rank through MCC counselling, usually around July-August.

items.title: State Quota (85%)
items.sub: 85% of seats are state-specific, run by state authorities by state rank, usually August-September. You appear in both.

items.title: Multiple rounds
items.sub: Three to six rounds depending on the state. Miss your choice in round one and later rounds plus floating seats give more chances.

items.title: Deemed & private
items.sub: Deemed universities accept NEET scores but run their own counselling. Fees vary hugely, from a few lakh to ₹25 lakh a year.

steps.title: Months 1-3: Class 11 base
steps.desc: Finish Physics Mechanics, Physical Chemistry, and core Biology like Cell Biology and Human Physiology. One chapter test a week.

steps.title: Months 4-6: Class 12
steps.desc: Cover Electrostatics, Optics and Modern Physics, Organic and Inorganic Chemistry, and Genetics and Evolution. Keep testing chapter-wise.

steps.title: Months 7-9: Revision + PYQs
steps.desc: Second and third NCERT Biology readings, daily Physics formula revision, and ten years of previous papers. Two full mocks a week.

steps.title: Months 10-12: Final push
steps.desc: A full mock daily with deep analysis, fourth and fifth NCERT readings, and no new topics in the last two weeks. Sleep and health matter now.

extra_sections.heading: NEET coaching - is it necessary?
content: NEET coaching costs Rs 1-4 lakh for 2-year programs at institutes like Allen, Aakash, and FIITJEE. Online coaching from Physics Wallah costs Rs 15,000-30,000.
Self-study with NCERT + reference books costs under Rs 5,000. The question is whether coaching adds enough value to justify the cost.

Data point: In NEET 2024, approximately 70% of top 1,000 rankers had coaching backgrounds (Allen and Aakash dominate). However, 30% were self-study students who relied on NCERT + free YouTube lectures (Physics Wallah, Unacademy).

The percentage of self-study toppers has been increasing as free resources improve in quality. When coaching helps: Structured study schedule (class timings enforce discipline), doubt-clearing sessions (immediate answers to conceptual questions), competitive environment (daily tests create exam pressure), and test series (professionally designed mock tests with detailed analysis).

When coaching doesn't help: If you're a self-disciplined student who can follow a study plan independently, coaching mainly provides social motivation, not unique content. The smart approach: Use free resources (Physics Wallah YouTube, NCERT PDFs, NEET PYQ apps) for content learning.
Buy a paid test series from Allen, Aakash, or Unacademy for Rs 3,000-5,000 for mock tests and performance analysis. This gives you 80% of coaching benefits at 5% of the cost.
The saved money can go toward your MBBS college fees.

extra_sections.heading: MBBS career - what comes after NEET
content: MBBS is a 5.5-year program (4.5 years academic + 1 year compulsory internship). During MBBS, you study Anatomy, Physiology, Biochemistry (pre-clinical years), Pathology, Pharmacology, Microbiology, Forensic Medicine (para-clinical years), and Medicine, Surgery, OB-GYN, Pediatrics, Ophthalmology, ENT, Dermatology, Psychiatry, Orthopedics (clinical years).

The curriculum is intense - 8-10 hours of classes and clinical postings daily. After MBBS: You appear for NEXT (National Exit Test - replacing the old NEET PG from 2025 onwards) to get a medical license AND apply for PG specialization simultaneously.

Popular PG specializations: General Medicine, General Surgery, Orthopedics, Dermatology, Radiology, Ophthalmology. Dermatology and Radiology are the most competitive due to lifestyle + income combination.
MBBS salary: Government medical officer starts at Rs 60,000-80,000/month (varies by state). After PG specialization, salary jumps to Rs 1-2 lakh/month in government hospitals.
Private practice after PG can earn Rs 2-10 lakh/month depending on specialization and location. Dermatologists and cosmetic surgeons in metros earn Rs 5-15 lakh/month from private practice.

MBBS + USMLE (USA medical licensing): Many Indian MBBS graduates pursue USMLE Steps 1, 2, and 3 to practice in the USA. This requires 2-3 years of preparation alongside MBBS, followed by residency matching in USA hospitals.
Indian doctors in the USA earn $200,000-400,000/year (Rs 1.6-3.2 crore). This pathway is increasingly popular among students from top medical colleges.
For more details, see our guide on UGC NET 2026. For more details, see our guide on JEE Main 2026.

extra_sections.heading: Books and resources for NEET
content: Biology: NCERT Class 11-12 (mandatory - THE primary source), MTG Objective Biology (NCERT-based MCQs), Trueman's Biology Vol 1 and 2 (additional practice), Biology Race by MTG (previous year papers chapterwise). NCERT alone covers 90% of NEET Biology - don't waste time on advanced books like Campbell or Lehninger.

Physics: HC Verma Concepts of Physics (concept building), DC Pandey Objective Physics (NEET-level MCQ practice), NCERT Class 11-12 Physics (for theory and direct NCERT-based questions). Focus on NCERT examples and exercise problems first - 15-20 NEET Physics questions are direct NCERT variants every year.

Chemistry: NCERT Class 11-12 Chemistry (mandatory), VK Jaiswal Inorganic Chemistry (additional practice), MS Chouhan Organic Chemistry (mechanism practice), Narendra Awasthi Physical Chemistry (numerical practice). For Inorganic, NCERT is 95% sufficient - don't buy additional inorganic books.

Free resources: Physics Wallah NEET playlist on YouTube (400+ hours of free lectures covering entire syllabus), NTA Abhyas app (official NEET mock test app - free), previous year NEET papers from neet.nta.nic.in (15+ years available for free), Allen NEET test series (paid but worth the investment at Rs 3,000-5,000).

extra_sections.heading: NEET 2026 expected schedule
extra_sections.content:
NEET 2026 was held on 3 May 2026, but NTA cancelled that paper after a question-paper leak. A re-exam is scheduled for 21 June 2026, with admit cards out and no extra fee for registered candidates.

Treat all dates as provisional and confirm them at neet.nta.nic.in.

extra_sections.heading: NCERT is the NEET answer key
extra_sections.content:
90% of NEET questions come from NCERT textbooks - many are exact NCERT statements rephrased as MCQs. Students who read NCERT 5 times score 550+.

Students who rely on coaching notes and skip NCERT score 400-450. There is no substitute for NCERT in NEET preparation.

Read it line by line, word by word, diagram by diagram.

extra_sections.text: 20 lakh students appear for NEET every year. Only 1 lakh get government MBBS seats. The difference between selection and rejection is often just 10-15 marks - which is 3-4 questions. Every single question matters. Every NCERT line matters.

extra_sections.heading: Exam day strategy - maximize your score in 200 minutes
content: Recommended sequence: Start with Biology (most scoring, builds confidence). Allocate 80 minutes for 90 Biology questions - that's about 53 seconds per question.
Biology questions are factual recall - you either know the answer or you don't. Don't spend more than 1 minute on any Biology question.
Mark uncertain ones and return later. Next, Chemistry (moderate difficulty).

Allocate 55 minutes. Start with Inorganic (fastest - direct NCERT recall), then Physical Chemistry (formula-based - if you know the formula, 30 seconds per question), then Organic (reaction-based - may need more thinking time).
Chemistry should give you 130-150 marks if you've prepared well. Last, Physics (hardest section for most NEET aspirants).
Allocate 65 minutes. Start with theory-based MCQs from Modern Physics and Optics (quick answers).
Then solve numerical problems from Mechanics and Electrostatics. Skip any problem that needs more than 3 minutes of calculation - return to it only if time permits.

Negative marking management: NEET deducts 1 mark for wrong MCQs. If you can eliminate 2 out of 4 options, guess between the remaining 2 - expected value is positive (+1.5 marks per question on average).
If all 4 options seem equally likely, SKIP - random guessing costs you on average. Target: attempt 160-170 questions out of 180 with 75%+ accuracy.

extra_sections.heading: NEET for reserved category candidates
content: Category-wise cutoff difference is significant in NEET. General category AIQ cutoff for government MBBS: typically 600-620.

These gaps translate to thousands of rank positions - a 550-scoring ST candidate gets better college options than a 620-scoring general candidate. Reserved category advantages: 15% AIQ seats have separate cutoffs for OBC (27%), SC (15%), ST (7.5%), and EWS (10%).
State quota seats also follow reservation. Some states like Tamil Nadu have 69% reservation - leaving only 31% for general category (open competition).

If you belong to a reserved category, ensure your caste certificate is valid and correctly issued. Common mistakes by reserved candidates: Not submitting the caste certificate in the correct central government format (state format certificates are rejected for AIQ counselling), not getting the latest OBC-NCL certificate (must be issued within 1 year and specifically mention non-creamy layer), and not applying through both AIQ AND state counselling (apply to both to maximize options).
PwD (Persons with Disability) reservation: 5% horizontal reservation across all categories. PwD candidates with 40%+ disability get relaxed cutoff and separate seat allocation.
The disability certificate must be from a government hospital's medical board. PwD candidates also get additional exam time (compensatory time) during NEET.

items.title: BDS (Dental)
items.sub: Also through NEET, with cutoffs 100-150 marks below MBBS. Government dentist pay is comparable to a government medical officer.

items.title: BAMS / BHMS / BUMS
items.sub: Ayurveda, Homeopathy and Unani, admitted through NEET at much lower cutoffs. You practise as a registered AYUSH doctor.

items.title: BSc Nursing
items.sub: An underrated path with strong international demand. Nursing salaries abroad can reach tens of lakhs a year.

items.title: BVSc (Veterinary)
items.sub: Through NEET at cutoffs around 400-500. High demand in livestock, pet clinics and the dairy industry.

extra_sections.heading: NEET helpline and official resources
content: Official NEET portal: neet.nta.nic.in for registration, admit card download, results, and counselling links. NTA helpline: 011-40759000 or email neet@nta.ac.in for exam-related queries.
MCC counselling portal: mcc.nic.in for AIQ counselling registration and seat allotment. State counselling portals vary by state - check your state's Directorate of Medical Education website.

For NEET preparation doubts: NTA Abhyas app (free official mock tests), NCERT textbooks free at ncert.nic.in, Physics Wallah YouTube channel (free complete NEET course with 20+ million subscribers). For counselling guidance: use college predictor tools on Shiksha.com and CareerGuru360 - enter your NEET score to see likely college options across AIQ and state counselling.

preparation_tips: NCERT is the BIBLE for NEET - 90-95% of questions come directly from NCERT 11th and 12th textbooks. Biology questions often come word-for-word from NCERT diagrams and definitions. Read NCERT Biology line-by-line multiple times. Successful NEET toppers read NCERT Bio 7-10 times before exam. Memorize diagrams, definitions, and classification systems verbatim.

Biology is your scoring subject - it's 50% of total marks (360/720). Most NEET toppers score 340-360 in Biology. Physics is toughest for aspirants (average: 120-150). Chemistry is middle (average: 140-170). Strategic approach: Dedicate 40% of prep time to Biology, 30% to Chemistry, 30% to Physics. This gives you Biology: 340+, Chemistry: 150+, Physics: 130+ = 620+ (99+ percentile).

Physics requires conceptual clarity from HC Verma or Physics Wallah videos, followed by MCQ practice from question banks. Don't memorize physics - understand principles. Focus on: Mechanics (25%), Optics (15%), Electrostatics+Current (20%), Modern Physics (10%), Thermodynamics (10%). Ignore advanced topics like superconductivity. Physics is only 25% of NEET - master the high-frequency chapters.

Chemistry has three components: Inorganic (reactions, periodic table), Organic (mechanisms, named reactions), Physical (thermodynamics, kinetics). Inorganic requires fact memorization - use charts, tables, periodic table notes. Organic requires understanding reaction mechanisms - MS Chouhan book is standard. Physical requires formula-based problem solving. Allocate prep: 30% Inorganic, 35% Organic, 35% Physical.

Practice with OMR sheets - NEET is offline pen-and-paper. Bubble filling speed and accuracy matter. Filling wrong bubbles or skipping bubbles causes mark loss. Practice with printed OMR sheets weekly. Time pressure is real - 3h 20m for 200 questions = 1 minute per question average. Time management: spend 1-1.5 minutes on easy questions, skip hard ones initially, revisit if time permits.

faqs.question: Is NEET the only way to become a doctor in India?
faqs.answer:
Yes, NEET is mandatory for MBBS/BDS admission in all government and private medical colleges in India. Even AIIMS and JIPMER, which historically had their own exams, now accept NEET scores.

The only alternative: Study MBBS abroad (China, Philippines, Russia) and clear FMGE (Foreign Medical Graduates Exam) to practice in India. But this is costly (₹20-40 lakh) and has lower success rate on FMGE than clearing NEET and studying in India.

faqs.question: How many times can I attempt NEET?
faqs.answer:
Currently, no official limit on attempts. You can appear every year as long as you meet age eligibility (minimum 17 years as of Dec 31).

Many successful NEET candidates clear it on 2nd or 3rd attempt. Dropping a year for NEET preparation is socially acceptable in India - many aspirants take deliberate breaks to focus.

However, realize that scores don't carry over - each year is a fresh exam.

faqs.question: NEET vs JEE - which is harder?
faqs.answer:
Different skill types. JEE tests conceptual application and problem-solving at advanced levels.

NEET tests memory, depth of knowledge, and standard-level problem solving. JEE seats per applicant: 0.5%.

NEET seats per applicant: 4.4%. Statistically, JEE is harder to crack, but subjectively, NEET has tougher competition numbers.

A student weak in logical reasoning should choose NEET (Biology-based); a student weak in memorization should choose JEE (concept-based).

faqs.question: Can I get MBBS with 500 marks out of 720?
faqs.answer:
500/720 (69.4%) gets you a government MBBS seat in many states through state quota counselling, especially in less competitive states (NE states, J&K, Tier-2 state capitals). For competitive states (Delhi, UP, Rajasthan), you need 550+ for government MBBS.

For private colleges, 500 is sufficient for admissions. For BDS (dental), 500 is excellent - you'll get government BDS in most states.

Score 500 is 97 percentile approximately - sufficient for medical education, not for top colleges.

faqs.question: What's the cost of MBBS in India?
faqs.answer:
Government MBBS: ₹10,000-1,00,000/year (total 5.5 years = ₹50,000-5,00,000). Private MBBS: ₹5-25 lakh/year (total 5.5 years = ₹27-137 lakh).

However, education loans cover 100% of fees at low interest (6-7%). Post-MBBS salary starts ₹60,000/month as junior doctor.

After MD/MS (specialization), income reaches ₹1,00,000+/month. ROI calculation: Loan repaid in 2-3 years.

MBBS is a high-ROI investment.

faqs.question: I scored 90 percentile in NEET. Can I get government MBBS?
faqs.answer:
90 percentile is approximately 545+ marks - yes, you qualify for government MBBS in most states through state quota counselling. However, actual college allocation depends on your state rank and state-specific cutoffs.

In competitive states (Delhi, Tamil Nadu), 90 percentile may not secure top government colleges but will secure mid-tier colleges. In less competitive states, 90 percentile secures good government MBBS.

Always research your state's previous year cutoffs.

faqs.question: How many attempts are allowed in NEET?
faqs.answer:
There is no limit on NEET attempts. You can appear any number of times as long as you meet the age criteria (minimum 17 years, no upper age limit as per current Supreme Court ruling).

Many successful doctors cleared NEET on their 2nd or 3rd attempt. Each attempt is independent - your best score in the appearing year is considered.

faqs.question: Is NEET conducted in Hindi?
faqs.answer:
Yes. NEET is available in 13 languages: English, Hindi, Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu.

Choose your medium of instruction at school as NEET language. However, NCERT Biology in English uses specific terminology - if you study in English medium, answering in English is easier.

faqs.question: Can I get MBBS with 500 marks in NEET?
faqs.answer:
Yes - but options are limited for general category. 500/720 typically gets state government college seats in states with more medical colleges (AP, Telangana, TN, Karnataka) through state counselling.

In high-competition states (UP, Bihar, Rajasthan), 500 may only get private college seats. For SC/ST/OBC, 500 marks comfortably gets government MBBS in most states.

faqs.question: What is the NEET cutoff for AIIMS Delhi?
faqs.answer:
AIIMS Delhi (through NEET AIQ) requires approximately 700-715 marks for MBBS - essentially near-perfect score. Other AIIMS (Jodhpur, Bhopal, Patna, Raipur, Rishikesh) need 680-700.

These are the most competitive medical seats in India. Realistic target for most NEET aspirants should be 600+ (good government college) rather than 700+ (AIIMS Delhi).

faqs.question: What is the full form of NEET UG?
faqs.answer: NEET UG stands for National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate). It is the single national entrance for MBBS, BDS and AYUSH courses, conducted by the NTA.

faqs.question: Was NEET 2026 cancelled and when is the re-exam?
faqs.answer:
NTA cancelled the 3 May 2026 paper after a question-paper leak. A re-exam is scheduled for 21 June 2026, and registered candidates can appear without any extra fee.

Always confirm the latest status at neet.nta.nic.in.
